rawInput.complaint: A 32‐year‐old Asian man presented with a 1‐year history of a right neck mass. His past medical history was noncontributory. On extraoral examination, there was a soft, slightly movable mass in the right submandibular region with normal overlying skin; the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable. Computed tomography of the neck revealed a well‐defined, mixed‐density lesion measuring approximately 5 × 3 cm adjacent to the right submandibular gland. Subsequent image segmentation suggested that the lesion contained components of fat, connective tissue, and osteoid. Primary differential diagnoses based on imaging included pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland, teratoma, and osteo/chondroid lipoma.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is a slowly enlarging right neck mass present for 1 year in a 32-year-old man. The patient’s concern is a persistent submandibular-region mass rather than pain, infection, or systemic illness. The chronic time course and lack of other symptoms immediately suggest a benign, slow-growing soft tissue or salivary-region neoplasm rather than an acute inflammatory process.

Salient positive findings are: (1) a soft, slightly movable mass in the right submandibular region, (2) normal overlying skin, (3) otherwise unremarkable physical examination, and (4) CT showing a well-defined 5 × 3 cm mixed-density lesion adjacent to the right submandibular gland. Importantly, image segmentation suggested the lesion contains fat, connective tissue, and osteoid. That combination strongly points toward a mesenchymal tumor with adipose and osseous/chondroid differentiation. The lesion is well circumscribed and clinically mobile, which supports a benign process.

Pertinent negatives include no mention of pain, tenderness, rapid growth, skin changes, ulceration, cranial nerve deficits, constitutional symptoms, or other abnormal examination findings. These negatives make infectious lymphadenitis, aggressive salivary malignancy, and metastatic nodal disease less likely. There is also no history suggesting congenital presentation, which somewhat argues against teratoma, although adult teratomas can occur.

Considering the candidate differentials:

1. Pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland: This is a reasonable initial consideration because the mass is in the submandibular region, is slow growing, well defined, and clinically benign-appearing. Pleomorphic adenoma can contain myxochondroid stromal elements and may appear heterogeneous on imaging. However, the lesion is described as adjacent to the submandibular gland rather than clearly arising within it, and the imaging segmentation specifically identified fat, connective tissue, and osteoid. A substantial fat component is not typical for pleomorphic adenoma, making this less fitting overall.

2. Teratoma: Teratoma can produce a mixed-density mass containing fat and calcified/osseous elements, so the imaging composition does fit. However, cervical teratomas are much more typical in infants and children, and in adults they are uncommon. The case provides no additional features of a complex congenital germ cell tumor beyond mixed tissue density. Thus teratoma remains plausible but less likely than a benign adipocytic tumor with osseous/chondroid metaplasia.

3. Osteo/chondroid lipoma: This diagnosis fits especially well because these rare benign lipomatous tumors are well circumscribed and composed of mature adipose tissue with chondroid and/or osseous matrix. The CT suggestion of fat, connective tissue, and osteoid is highly characteristic. The soft, slightly movable, slow-growing nature over 1 year also supports a benign lipomatous lesion. The submandibular region is an unusual but recognized soft tissue location for such a tumor.

Narrowing to the single most likely diagnosis, the decisive feature is the lesion composition on imaging: fat plus osteoid/connective tissue in a well-defined benign-appearing neck mass. Among the listed differentials, osteo/chondroid lipoma best integrates the adipose and osseous/chondroid elements while matching the indolent clinical behavior. Pleomorphic adenoma explains the location but not the fat-rich composition as well, and teratoma explains mixed tissues but is less typical in this adult presentation. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is osteochondrolipoma (osteo/chondroid lipoma).

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Well-defined, soft, slightly movable, slow-growing submandibular-region mass with CT/image segmentation showing fat, connective tissue, and osteoid—features characteristic of a benign lipomatous tumor with osseous/chondroid differentiation.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Pleomorphic adenoma of the submandibular gland
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Slow-growing, well-defined mass adjacent to the submandibular gland in the submandibular region is compatible with a benign salivary tumor, but the prominent fat component is less typical.
Mixed-density lesion containing fat and osteoid/calcified elements can occur in teratoma, but adult cervical teratoma is uncommon and the presentation otherwise favors a benign mesenchymal tumor.
